summary: Phenolphthalein is a diphenylmethane stimulant (contact) laxative that was for decades a common over-the-counter remedy for constipation. It increases intestinal motility and fluid secretion, producing a bowel movement several hours after an oral dose. It is no longer marketed in the United States: the FDA proposed reclassifying it as not generally recognized as safe and effective for OTC use after animal carcinogenicity studies raised concerns, and manufacturers withdrew or reformulated phenolphthalein-containing products in the late 1990s. It characteristically turns alkaline urine and stool pink-red, which is harmless. This record is historical/educational and reflects FDA action and the former OTC laxative monograph.

moa: Phenolphthalein is a contact/stimulant laxative. After oral absorption and enterohepatic recirculation it acts on the colonic mucosa to stimulate peristalsis and to increase secretion of water and electrolytes into the bowel lumen, producing a laxative effect several hours later. Its prolonged enterohepatic cycling accounts for a relatively long duration of action.

absolute: Intestinal obstruction, ileus or undiagnosed acute abdominal pain
Appendicitis or symptoms suggestive of it
No longer marketed/approved in the US (withdrawn over carcinogenicity concerns)
relative: Chronic use or laxative abuse (risk of electrolyte loss, dependence, melanosis coli)
monitor: Fluid and electrolyte status with chronic or excessive use

preg: Avoid - phenolphthalein is not recommended in pregnancy, and stimulant laxatives in general are second-line; the product has in any case been withdrawn from the US market. Bulk-forming or osmotic laxatives are preferred when treatment is needed in pregnancy.
lact: Avoid - some of the drug/active metabolite may be excreted in breast milk and could affect the infant's bowel; the product is no longer marketed. Bulk-forming or osmotic laxatives are preferred during breastfeeding.
renal: Use with caution; the main concern is fluid and electrolyte loss (including potassium) with excessive or prolonged use, which is more hazardous in renal impairment.
hepatic: Use with caution; phenolphthalein undergoes enterohepatic recirculation and is conjugated in the liver, which may be altered in hepatic impairment.

major: Excessive use causing hypokalemia can potentiate digoxin toxicity
Hypokalemia from overuse may enhance the effect of neuromuscular blocking agents and increase arrhythmia risk with some drugs
moderate: Other drugs that lower potassium (diuretics, corticosteroids) - additive electrolyte loss with chronic use
May reduce absorption of other oral medicines by speeding intestinal transit

interactions.food: May be taken without regard to food; adequate fluid intake was advised.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction, but avoid combining with chronic laxative misuse.
interactions.diagnostics: Turns alkaline urine and stool pink-red, which can interfere with visual interpretation of urinalysis and stool examination; may affect some phenolsulfonphthalein (PSP) and urinary tests.

Theoretical carcinogenicity concern based on animal studies (basis for US withdrawal)

missed: Phenolphthalein was used as needed for occasional constipation rather than on a fixed schedule, so there is no scheduled dose to make up. The product is in any case no longer marketed in the US; do not attempt to obtain or re-dose it - use a currently approved laxative instead.
overdose: Overdose or chronic overuse causes profuse diarrhea with abdominal cramps and can lead to dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, particularly hypokalemia (with weakness, cardiac arrhythmias and, in severe cases, cardiovascular collapse). Management is supportive: stop the drug, rehydrate, and correct fluid and electrolyte losses (especially potassium) with monitoring.
